name: 萬馬軒 新宿西口本店 (Manbaken Shinjuku Nishiguchi Honten)

claims.text: The miso tare/soup base is described as combining pork-bone and chicken stock with a secret soy-sauce blend, indicating standard (wheat-containing) soy sauce is used; no wheat-free soy sauce alternative was mentioned.

No restaurant-specific statement on separating gluten-free (100% buckwheat) noodle boiling water from wheat-containing noodles or tempura batter was found; this is a traditional soba shop without a specialized allergen protocol.
No confirmation of a wheat-free (tamari) soy sauce; standard Japanese soy sauce used in soba tsuyu typically contains wheat.
The kitchen prepares shrimp and conger-eel tempura and bonito-based dashi alongside the soba, so cross-contact with animal products is likely for any vegan order.
The zaru soba is made with 100% buckwheat flour (namagona-uchi), meaning the noodle itself, unlike standard nihachi soba, contains no wheat binder.
The shoyu tare is standard Japanese soy sauce, which typically contains wheat; no wheat-free or gluten-free soy sauce alternative is documented for this shop.

The broth is intentionally made without added MSG or chemical seasoning (無化調), relying on whole-chicken stock and aromatics for flavor — a plus for diners sensitive to MSG, though unrelated to gluten or animal-product content.

name: 麺屋海神 新宿店 (Menya Kaijin Shinjuku)

claims.text: No gluten-free menu or process was found; noodles and multiple toppings contain wheat, so cross-contamination is essentially unavoidable in this kitchen.
Broth is fish-bone based (grilled fish scraps) and toppings include shrimp and chicken, so there is no vegan-safe base at this shop.
No gluten-free protocol, dedicated fryer, or wheat-free soy sauce mentioned in any source found; this is a conventional seafood izakaya kitchen with no allergen-specific accommodations documented.
Standard izakaya use of soy sauce is implied by dishes like sashimi, nameroo, and simmered fish, but no source confirms whether a wheat-free (tamari-style) soy sauce is available.
Menu is fish/seafood-centric (sashimi, grilled and simmered fish, sardine tsumire soup); no vegan-specific dishes or cross-contact information found.

Okonomiyaki and monjayaki are both wheat-flour-batter dishes cooked on a shared teppan grill used for all orders, so cross-contact with gluten is essentially unavoidable; no gluten-free batter or dedicated equipment was found in any source.
No vegetable-only or vegan course was identified; okonomiyaki/monjayaki are typically prepared with dashi-based sauces and shared teppan surfaces alongside meat and seafood items.

name: ネパリコ 渋谷店 (Nepalico Shibuya (Nepalico Dal Bhat & Cafe))

claims.text: No published information on dedicated gluten-free prep areas or cross-contamination controls; ask staff directly.

The vegetarian dal bhat set is described as dal soup, rice, three tarkari, three achar, sag, and papad — the fried papad wafer sits directly on the shared plate, an unconfirmed-composition wheat/cross-contact vector no source addresses.

Search across FindMeGlutenFree, HappyCow, Tripadvisor and the shop site returned no celiac/coeliac-specific review or any statement of GF handling for Nepalico Shibuya; 'gluten-free' appears only as a generic property of dal bhat as a dish.
Japanese allergen search confirms no gluten-free or wheat-allergen accommodation information is published for the store; users are told to phone the shop directly — i.e., no verified protocol exists.

The claim that the vegetarian set is dairy-free/vegan came only from an aggregated search summary, not any cited primary source; Nepali dal/tarkari/sag commonly use ghee, leaving vegan status unconfirmed.
No published information confirming whether the vegetarian Dal Bhat is prepared without ghee/dairy or shares cookware with meat curries; ask staff directly.
The Dal Bhat vegetarian set (dal soup, tarkari, two achar, rice) replaces the meat curry with extra vegetable/pickle sides, and at lunch the dal soup and rice are refilled free of charge.

name: 肉汁水餃子 餃包 新宿店 (Nikujiru Suigyoza Gyopao Shinjuku-ten (Juicy)

claims.text: No dedicated gluten-free prep area, fryer, or allergen protocol is confirmed; the kitchen's primary output is wheat-wrapper boiled dumplings, so cross-contact risk for a strict celiac diet is likely significant even when ordering the gluten-free chimaki item.

FindMeGlutenFree's Shinjuku directory returns no listing or celiac review for this dumpling shop, despite covering the area — there is no independent celiac-grade evidence that anyone has eaten here safely.

Aggregator coverage states the shop labels 餃子ソーセージ, 鶏肉チマキ, 油淋鶏 (deep-fried chicken) and 麻婆豆腐 as gluten-free. Yurinchi and mapo tofu conventionally use wheat soy sauce and wheat-flour coating/deep frying, contradicting the shop's unconfirmed GF-soy-sauce and no-dedicated-fryer status — indicating the 'GF' label reflects recipe wheat, not celiac cross-contact safety.

All gluten-free promotion originates from a single source — the restaurant's own 'おすすめ グルテンフリーの鶏肉チマキ' marketing blog — with no protocol, ppm, or dedicated-prep disclosure; secondary blogs only restate this shop-authored claim.

The shop is explicitly a 肉汁水餃子専門店 (juicy boiled water-dumpling specialty restaurant) whose entire production line is wheat wrappers, boiled in shared water — a structurally high cross-contact environment for celiac.
The restaurant has proactively promoted a gluten-free chicken chimaki on its own blog as a recommendation for gluten-sensitive guests, indicating at least some staff awareness of gluten-free demand.
